cultivar: Mixed large, medium and small-leaf old trees
processing: Made as sheng is generally: withered, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or kept loose. A local heritage maker claims a 72-step traditional method, a claim from promotion rather than a standard.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Yunnan old-tree tea.
appearance_dry: Mixed leaf sizes in one lot, dark green with some buds, reflecting the mixed garden.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaves of uneven size.
taste_profile: Sellers call it elegant rather than forceful: a faint bitterness that turns sweet, a smooth broth and a lasting clean aroma.

brewing.notes: Its reputation is for delicacy, so do not overload the gaiwan; a heavy dose hides what you paid for.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, with spring old-tree lots at the top. The gap is unusually wide: one published spring list gave 8,000 to 12,000 yuan/kg for large old trees and 200 to 300 for nearby small trees, so the name alone tells you little. Ask directly which trees the leaf came from.
description:
Kunlushan is an old tea garden in Ning'er County, Pu'er prefecture, and it is sold on two things: a tribute-tea story and an unusual mix of trees. Large, medium and small-leaf plants are said to grow side by side, in what one report calls a semi-cultivated old tree community.

Processing follows the sheng pattern of sun-dried maocha, then pressing. The mixed garden is the distinctive part, since a single lot may hold quite different leaf.

Descriptions favour one word, elegant: light bitterness turning sweet, a smooth broth, clean lingering aroma, set against stronger styles like Banzhang or Mengku. Those words come largely from sellers, so taste before trusting them. Use a modest dose and short steeps.

Be careful buying. Real old-tree tea from the garden is scarce and expensive, while the surrounding small-tree tea costs a tiny fraction of the price and can carry the same mountain name. A cheap Kunlushan cake is almost certainly not the tea the reputation rests on.
history:
Kunlushan is widely described as a royal tribute garden supplying the Qing court, and local accounts say palace records mention it. Treat the detail as a local tradition, since the specific archives are rarely cited. Its cultivated old trees are often given ages of over 400 years.

The garden is reported to have fallen into neglect after land was divided among households, until in 1987 the family of Li Xingchang, later a recognised intangible-heritage maker, contracted it. Kunlushan was named a Chinese traditional village in August 2013, and one account says the garden was listed as a Pu'er municipal heritage site in the same year.
